title: Oil Crisis Fuels Global EV Boom as 50 Countries Break Quarterly Sales Records
excerpt: The IEA says electric vehicles will account for 29 percent of global car sales in 2026, with India, Europe, and Latin America leading the surge.
body:
• Fifty countries posted quarterly EV sales records in Q2 2026, with global electrified vehicle sales rising 4 percent year-over-year according to the International Energy Agency
  • India, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea all hit new all-time highs for EV sales in the first half of 2026
  • The oil price spike from the US-Iran conflict is accelerating the shift, as road vehicles account for nearly half of global oil consumption
  • Global EV sales are now projected to reach 23 million in 2026, representing 29 percent of all new car sales worldwide
  • BYD overtook Tesla in Q2 with 557,090 battery-electric deliveries versus Tesla's 480,126

Oil Crisis Becomes EV Catalyst

The global oil crisis triggered by the US-Iran conflict has done what years of government subsidies struggled to accomplish: it has made millions of car buyers choose electric. Fifty countries set quarterly EV sales records in the second quarter of 2026, according to a new International Energy Agency report, with electrified vehicle sales climbing 4 percent year-over-year and 35 percent over the previous quarter.

The IEA now projects electric cars will account for 29 percent of all new vehicles sold worldwide this year, up from its earlier forecast of 28 percent. Global sales are expected to reach 23 million units in 2026, building on the 20 million sold in 2025.

Road vehicles account for nearly half of global oil use, making the sector particularly exposed to fuel price spikes and supply disruptions.

International Energy Agency

India Among the Breakout Markets

India recorded its highest-ever quarterly EV sales, part of a broader surge across emerging markets. Sales of electric two- and three-wheelers more than doubled year-on-year in Southeast Asia during Q1, and grew more than 30 percent in India. Brazil, Australia, and South Korea also posted all-time highs in the first half of 2026.

Europe delivered the strongest regional performance among mature markets, with EV sales jumping nearly 30 percent year-over-year in Q1. The UK saw a 35 percent increase in battery-electric registrations, with BEVs and PHEVs now comprising 36 percent of all new car registrations. France and Germany led Europe's top five markets with growth of 50 and 41 percent respectively, boosted by renewed government purchase incentives.

BYD Retakes the Crown From Tesla

The quarter also saw BYD reclaim the global battery-electric vehicle sales lead from Tesla. The Chinese automaker sold 557,090 passenger BEVs in Q2, compared with Tesla's 480,126 deliveries, a gap of nearly 77,000 vehicles. For the first half of 2026, BYD leads with 867,479 passenger BEV sales against Tesla's 838,149.

Tesla's numbers were still strong in context. Its Q2 deliveries rose 24.9 percent year-over-year, with the Model 3 and Model Y accounting for more than 97 percent of volume. But BYD's scale across a broader product range, including plug-in hybrids that push its total new-energy vehicle count far higher, gives it structural advantages in markets like China, where electric cars now account for nearly 60 percent of total sales.

The China Paradox

China presents a complex picture. While it remains the world's largest EV market by far, its BEV sales actually fell 20 percent year-over-year in Q1 2026, dragging global figures into negative territory for the quarter. The decline followed policy changes that reduced purchase subsidies. But preliminary April data showed a sharp rebound, with monthly electric car sales growing to a record-high share of over 60 percent of total car sales.

The country is also building more EVs than it can sell domestically. An estimated one million electric vehicles currently sit unsold, even as Chinese manufacturers like BYD expand exports aggressively. The share of electric cars in China's car exports rose from about 35 percent in 2025 to more than 45 percent in the first half of 2026.

A Structural Shift

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol pointed to falling battery prices and potential policy responses to the energy crisis as drivers of continued momentum. The agency projects the global EV fleet could grow from nearly 80 million vehicles today to as many as 510 million by 2035, even without additional policy announcements. For consumers in countries like India, where fuel price sensitivity is high and motorization rates are still low, the economics of going electric have never been more compelling.
